payload.theorem_nl: Let $p$ be a prime number greater than $3$. For each $k \\in \\{1,\\dots,p-1\\}$, let $I(k) \\in \\{1,2,\\dots,p-1\\}$ be such that $k \\cdot I(k) \\equiv 1 \\pmod{p}$. Prove that the number of integers $k \\in \\{1,\\dots,p-2\\}$ such that $I(k+1) < I(k)$ is greater than $p/4-1$.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix a prime p > 3. First use the standard modular-inverse fact to define the map I(k) uniquely for each k in {1,...,p-1}, and hence define the descent set S = {k in {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k)}. Reduce the goal to proving the stronger integral estimate |S| >= floor(p/4), because that implies |S| > p/4 - 1. Next split into two exhaustive cases. If p >= 1000, apply the global analytic lower bound for descents of the inverse permutation, namely |S| >= (p-3)/2 - 2*sqrt(p)*log(p), and then apply the explicit arithmetic inequality showing that this quantity is at least floor(p/4) for every prime p >= 1000. If instead 5 <= p < 1000, apply the finite verification lemma, which already gives |S| >= floor(p/4) for every prime in this range; this includes the boundary prime p = 5 that caused a gap in earlier decompositions. Since these two cases cover all primes p > 3, we obtain |S| >= floor(p/4) in full generality. Finally convert this to the exact theorem statement |S| > p/4 - 1.
